analysis.one_liner: Lets the post office offer basic banking, small-dollar loans, and money transfers at low cost.
analysis.headline: The Postal Banking Act, sponsored by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand with two cosponsors, was referred to a Senate committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would direct the U.S. Postal Service to offer basic banking at its branches: small checking and savings accounts, low-cost small-dollar loans of up to $500, debit cards, check cashing, and domestic and international money transfers. The Postal Service would set the rates and fees itself, with small-loan rates capped near the Treasury's short-term borrowing rate, and it would be required to offer these services directly, not through contracts with private banks. The Federal Reserve would transfer the Postal Service enough money to make the services substantially reduce the number of people who lack bank accounts or rely on payday lenders and check-cashing stores.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 7 million U.S. households with no bank account, plus millions more who pay high fees for check cashing, payday loans, overdraft charges, and remittances. The Postal Service, which has branch locations in many towns and neighborhoods where banks have closed, would gain a new public mission and a funding stream from the Federal Reserve to run it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Unbanked and underbanked households; payday borrowers

how_it_helps.text: The Postal Service would be authorized to provide small checking and savings accounts (up to $20,000 per account), debit cards, online banking, check cashing, bill pay, and domestic and international money transfers at its branches.

It could make low-cost small-dollar loans of up to $500 at a time ($1,000 within a year of the first loan), with the total rate for such loans capped at slightly above the Treasury 1-month rate — far below typical payday loan pricing.

The Postal Service would set its own rates and fees, required to give customer access and the public interest significant consideration, and savings interest rates would have to be at least 100 percent of the FDIC national savings rate.

The Federal Reserve Board would transfer the Postal Service whatever sums are necessary, in an amount sufficient to substantially decrease the number of people who are unbanked or who use payday lending, check cashing, prepaid debit cards, and overdrafts.
The bill requires these services to be provided directly by the Postal Service, not through a partnership or contract with private banks or other financial institutions.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, check-cashing stores, and banks that collect overdraft and low-balance account fees would lose customers and revenue. The Federal Reserve — and ultimately the public — would bear the funding risk if the new services cost more than they earn. The Postal Service would take on a line of business with little operating history.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, check cashers, banks with fee income

drawbacks.text: The Postal Service would have to provide services directly, with no bank charter and no private partnerships, and would be funded through Federal Reserve transfers; if the new services lose money, those losses would sit on a public balance sheet.

Loan rates would be capped near the Treasury 1-month rate, well below what small-dollar lending typically costs to make, so the loan book would likely operate at a loss that the Fed would have to cover.

The Postal Service has no experience making loans, and it has faced years of financial losses in its core mail business; adding a lending operation could add operating and credit risk to an already strained institution.
Small-dollar loans would be capped at $500 at a time, which limits how much debt relief the program could provide to borrowers with larger needs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households now paying triple-digit annual rates on payday loans or steep check-cashing and remittance fees, the benefit would be direct and immediate, and the bill's structure (no bank charter, direct provision, Fed funding) was deliberately designed to keep it a public service. The main honest objection is cost and execution risk: subsidized loan rates plus an inexperienced lender could mean recurring losses funded by the Federal Reserve, and the Postal Service's own financial troubles raise questions about whether it could run a consumer lending business well. The bill tried to manage this with annual GAO reporting on who uses the products and at what balances, but the core funding bet was untested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 22, 2022, read twice, and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Postal Banking Act in the Senate on March 22, 2022, with Sens. Bernie Sanders and Jeff Merkley as the bill's two cosponsors.
On the day of introduction, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
That was the bill's last action: the full action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further movement before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, check-cashing stores, and banks collecting overdraft and low-balance fees kept the market to themselves, and the Postal Service was spared the risk of running a new banking operation; unbanked households got no relief from high-cost small-dollar credit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders and banks kept the fee market

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Postal Banking Act in the Senate on March 22, 2022.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 22, 2022 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, and no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Banking and payday lending industries
against.role: Banks, payday lenders, and check-cashing firms that earn fees from unbanked and underbanked customers
against.what_they_did: Opposed postal banking proposals, which would put a low-cost public alternative between them and their fee-paying customers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; all three supporting senators were Democrats or Independents, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: A Postal Service loan of up to $500 with total interest capped near the Treasury 1-month rate would directly undercut triple-digit-rate payday loans. The bill's stated goal was to substantially decrease use of payday lending.
The post office would offer check cashing and domestic and foreign money transfers, replacing services that now charge percentage-based fees to people without bank accounts.

Overdraft fees, low-balance account fees, and prepaid card charges are a major revenue source tied to underbanked customers; free-standing postal accounts and debit cards would draw those customers away. The bill also bars the Postal Service from offering services through private banks, so banks gain no role.

The Postal Service would gain a new public line of business funded by Federal Reserve transfers, using its unmatched branch network — often the only financial presence left in bank deserts. Its interest in running the service runs alongside the public's.
